claims.text: The starting material is a single-phase disordered high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
Increasing atomic size mismatch in a high-entropy alloy increases local lattice distortion.
Greater local lattice distortion strengthens electron-phonon coupling.
The distortion-induced change in electron-phonon coupling alters the density of low-energy vibrational modes and causes phonon softening.
Distortion-mediated changes in electron-phonon coupling and phonons modify the superconducting transition temperature.
Superconductivity in the baseline alloy follows a conventional BCS mechanism with established electron-phonon coupling.
The baseline alloy has a known superconducting transition temperature.
Increasing atomic size mismatch while retaining a single disordered phase will produce a measurable change in phonon characteristics relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy will have a superconducting transition temperature measurably different from that of the baseline alloy.
Identical low-temperature synthesis conditions ensure a uniform disordered solid-solution structure in all samples.
Vibrational spectroscopy can reveal the predicted phonon softening and be used to assess changes in electron-phonon coupling.
Chemical bonding and electronic-structure changes may compete with size-mismatch effects in determining superconductivity.
The hypothesis applies only while the modified and baseline alloys remain single-phase disordered solid solutions under identical synthesis and measurement conditions.
A joint absence of phonon softening and a statistically distinguishable Tc change in the higher-mismatch alloys would falsify the proposed mechanism.
